newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major reels as top tabloid backs Blair.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major reels as top tabloid backs Blair.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's re-election hopes suffered an early blow on Monday when Britain's best-selling newspaper, The Sun, threw its support behind Labour leader Tony Blair.

Hours after Major launched Britain's longest election campaign in 80 years by confirming that polling would take place on May 1, The Sun described his ruling Conservative party as "tired, divided and rudderless."

Under the headline "The Sun Backs Blair", Tuesday's edition of the tabloid, owned by Australian-born media magnate Rupert Murdoch, will say in an editorial: "In six weeks' time, Britain will vote for a government to take it into the 21st century.
"The people need a leader with vision, purpose and courage who can inspire them and fire their imaginations. The Sun believes that man is Tony Blair."

The Sun, which sells more than four million copies a day, boasted after Major came from behind to win the 1992 election that its support had tipped the balance. "It's The Sun Wot Won It," it crowed then.
Conservative strategists put a brave face on the paper's switch of heart and said they were confident of pulling off an unprecedented fifth consecutive election victory.
After announcing the date of the election, Major immediately plunged into the campaign, pulling out his trusty soapbox to take his message to voters in Luton, north of London.

Shouting to be heard above the din of protesters, Major said: "I have no shred of doubt that the five years to come will be five more Conservative years to carry on the revolution of the last 18 years."
"The last time I came to Luton I had a reception just like this and three weeks later we won both Luton seats and the general election," he yelled from his tiny makeshift stage.
Blair, Major's main opponent in what is shaping up as a U.S.-style presidential campaign, opened his bid for power in the cathedral city of Gloucester, western England.
"I think this election will be a battle between hope and fear," Blair, whose party leads the Conservatives in opinion polls by about 25 points, told a group of floating voters.

He has ditched virtually all of Labour's old socialist ideology to try to attract middle class votes in bellwether marginal seats like Gloucester which it must capture to win power for the first time since 1979.
"I do not think there is any danger of Labour reverting to the past. But I think the challenge is to prove that in office," Blair said.
Major said earlier that the 44-day campaign would be gruelling but fun.
"I believe this election is winnable. Not only do I think it's winnable, I think I'm going to win this election...We have an 18-year record record that I am proud of," he said.

But the opinion polls suggest Britons want a change after 18 years of Conservative rule that galvanised the economy but, in the eyes of the ruling party's critics, also increased inequalities and bred insecurity.
No party in power has ever clawed back such a big poll deficit as that facing the Conservativbes so close to a general election.
Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing to win power. This would be larger than any Labour has achieved since 1945 and Blair vowed to be "the eternal warrior against complacency."
Major may have lost the Sun's backing but he received a warm endorsement from his predecessor, Margaret Thatcher, who in the past has often sniped at him from the sidelines.
"Stay with us and with John Major until we cross the finishing line," she told reporters outside her London office.
